[THOUGHT] The patient is a young postpartum woman with increased urinary frequency and a subjective fever. Key positive exam finding is uterine tenderness on bimanual exam; cervical motion tenderness, uterine size, and lochia are reported as normal. Urinalysis results are essentially noncontributory (microscopy reported as normal), and the patient denies dysuria. Differential considerations include postpartum endometritis, urinary tract infection (cystitis or early pyelonephritis), bladder dysfunction/irritation related to postpartum state, and retained products causing secondary infection.

Postpartum endometritis classically presents in the early postpartum period with fever and uterine tenderness; foul lochia is common but not always present. Although C-section is the strongest risk factor, endometritis can occur after vaginal delivery, especially with prolonged or traumatic labor (the patient delivered an 11 lb infant, which may have increased operative/traumatic risk). The presence of uterine tenderness in a postpartum patient with subjective fever is the most specific clinical clue pointing to endometritis. A UTI would more typically cause dysuria, pyuria, or positive UA findings; here urine microscopy is normal, making UTI less likely. Other pelvic infections (e.g., pelvic abscess, retained products) would often have abnormal lochia or more pronounced pelvic findings; those are less supported by the current data.

Given the constellation of postpartum status, subjective fever, and focal uterine tenderness with otherwise noncontributory urinalysis, the single most likely diagnosis is postpartum endometritis.

[DIAGNOSIS]
Postpartum endometritis

[THOUGHT] The available data are insufficient to confidently diagnose postpartum endometritis. The classic diagnosis relies on maternal fever, uterine tenderness, and foul-smelling lochia in the postpartum period, or supporting lab/imaging showing infection/retained products. Here the patient has subjective fever (no measured temperature), uterine tenderness only, and normal lochia; many key history points (time since delivery, labor course, rupture of membranes, breastfeeding, wound status) and objective data (vital signs, CBC, urinalysis/culture results, pelvic ultrasound) are missing. Urinary frequency without dysuria could reflect UTI (urinalysis pending) or simply normal postpartum voiding—without the UA/culture you cannot exclude a urinary infection as the cause of symptoms. Red-flag assessments are also absent (measured fever, tachycardia, hypotension, severe pain, heavy bleeding) which would change urgency/management.

Red-flag/critical tests missing: measured temperature and full vital signs, urine dip/UA results and urine culture, CBC (WBC), timing since delivery and labor/ROM history, assessment of lochia odor/quantity over time, and pelvic ultrasound if retained products suspected. If any systemic signs (high fever, tachycardia, hypotension) are present, this requires urgent management.

[DECISION] INCOMPLETE

[FEEDBACK] Critical information required to support or refute postpartum endometritis (provide exact items):
1. Measured vital signs now (temperature, HR, BP, RR, O2 sat) and documentation of any fevers since delivery.
2. Exact time interval since delivery (days postpartum) and details of the delivery course (duration of labor, prolonged ROM, intrapartum fever, chorioamnionitis, instrumentation).
3. Complete urinalysis results (leukocyte esterase, nitrites, WBC/RBC on microscopy) and obtain a urine culture.
4. CBC with differential (WBC count, bands) and basic metabolic panel if systemic infection suspected.
5. Detailed description of lochia (amount, color, odor) and whether there is heavy or prolonged bleeding.
6. Pelvic ultrasound if retained products or intrauterine collection is a concern.
7. Focused reassessment for other infection sources: breast exam for mastitis/abscess, perineal/c-section wound exam if applicable.
8. If any systemic instability or high fever, blood cultures and urgent empiric antibiotics per obstetric infection protocols.

Collect these data before committing to a diagnosis of endometritis; alternatively, if UA/urine culture show bacteriuria consistent with UTI and no other signs of endometritis are present, treat as UTI.

Postpartum endometritis classically presents in the early postpartum period with fever and uterine tenderness; foul lochia is common but not always present. Postpartum endometritis
